title: Cells without HLA flags can still be attacked through the patient’s own immune cells
idea: Assume cells with no HLA flags cannot trigger memory T cells or antibodies.
why: Without HLA flags, T cells cannot see the cells directly. But the patient’s own immune cells can still pick up the graft’s debris and restart the attack.
check: Mix the patient’s immune cells with debris from flag-free islets, and look for T-cell activation and cell damage.
instead: Score the autoimmune test lower, shed less debris (small clusters, pre-built vessels) and test whether extra protection is needed.

title: A resting B2M promoter may give too little HLA-E and CD47 in the first hours
idea: Assume the natural B2M promoter gives 180,000 to 220,000 CD47 molecules per cell, as seen in cells made with a virus.
why: Resting beta cells make little B2M, so HLA-E and CD47 may be too low in the first 72 hours, when natural killer cells and macrophages attack.
check: Count CD47 and HLA-E per cell on resting and inflamed cells, then test the cells against natural killer cells and macrophages.
instead: Measure the level before relying on it. If it is too low, add a steady “on” switch such as GAPDH or AAVS1.

title: Constant, unregulated IL-10 production
idea: Make the cells produce IL-10 all the time to calm nearby T cells.
why: This is a cautious project decision rather than a proven failure. The one cited study is about mast cells in the gut, not islets. Better options exist: PD-L1 and SERPINB9.
check: Examine transplanted grafts for mast cells and other immune cells.
instead: Use PD-L1 and SERPINB9, switched on by the CXCL10 gene.

title: Switching off essential genes: PTPN2, TNFAIP3 and GAD2
idea: Switch off PTPN2, TNFAIP3 or GAD2 to avoid autoimmune attack.
why: People rarely lose these genes and stay healthy. PTPN2 and TNFAIP3 protect beta cells from dying, and GAD2 makes GABA, which keeps glucagon in check.
check: Expose the cells to inflammatory signals and count cell death. Measure glucagon release.
instead: Never switch them off. Switch off TYK2, or add TNFAIP3 or SERPINB9 instead.

title: Making several base or prime edits at once
idea: Assume several base or prime edits at once are risk-free.
why: Adenine base editors caused DNA rearrangements in the cited study. The project extends that concern to making several base and prime edits at once, as an engineering precaution.
check: Scan the edited cell lines for DNA rearrangements, using optical mapping, whole-genome sequencing or CAST-seq.
instead: Keep the simple design to zero base edits, and count each extra one against the score.

title: Keeping one HLA-C gene may not calm natural killer cells
idea: Assume keeping one HLA-C gene is enough to calm all natural killer cells.
why: HLA-C is made at about a tenth of the level of HLA-A and HLA-B. Without them, one HLA-C gene may not give enough of the signal that calms natural killer cells.
check: Test natural killer cells from different donors against the resting cells.
instead: Use the B2M, HLA-E and CD47 insert, or measure the signal before relying on HLA-C.

title: Switching off RNLS: more oxygen use, and no better insulin response
idea: Assume switching off RNLS always helps, based on a mouse cell study.
why: In human cells, RNLS-off cells still released insulin poorly and used more oxygen, which hurts large clusters.
check: Compare normal and RNLS-off cells for insulin release and oxygen use, in 120 µm and 200 µm clusters.
instead: Leave it out of the simple design and compare it in small clusters.

title: Switching off G6PC2 may cause low blood sugar between meals
idea: Switch off G6PC2 in every design to remove an autoimmune target.
why: G6PC2 helps set the blood sugar level at which insulin stops. Losing it may lower blood sugar between meals. This has not been seen in grafts, so it is a precaution.
check: Drop glucose from 16.7 to 2.8 mM and time how fast insulin stops. It must stop within 3 minutes.
instead: Leave it out of the simple design unless that check passes.

title: Putting the safety switch under a promoter only mature beta cells use
idea: Control the safety switch with the G6PC2 or INS promoter, so one edit does two jobs.
why: Those promoters only work in mature beta cells. Immature or rogue cells would not make the switch and could not be destroyed.
check: Mix 10% immature stem cells into the islets, add the drug AP1903 for 72 hours and count survivors. The proposed target is fewer than 1 in 100 million cells capable of regrowth.
instead: Put the switch on both copies of a safe location (AAVS1 or GAPDH) and check it works in every cell type.

title: Switching off STAT1 or JAK1 while relying on an interferon switch
idea: Switch off STAT1 or JAK1, and use an interferon-triggered switch to turn on PD-L1 and SERPINB9.
why: With STAT1 or JAK1 gone, the interferon signal never arrives, so the protection never turns on.
check: Treat normal and STAT1-off cells with inflammatory signals, then count PD-L1 on each cell.
instead: Keep a second trigger (NF-κB), as the CXCL10 gene does.
